# Nuclear reactor (controlled chain reaction) (`nuclear_reactor`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs nuclear_fission; helped by feedback_control, steam_turbine, radioactivity
- Core idea: When a uranium-235 nucleus splits it releases two or three fast neutrons. In natural uranium (0.7 % U-235) these are mostly lost unless they are slowed down, because slow neutrons are far more likely to split another U-235 nucleus. So lumps of uranium are spaced out in a moderator that slows neutrons without absorbing them: very pure graphite or heavy water (ordinary water only with enriched uranium). At criticality each generation of neutrons produces, on average, an equal next generation and power stays steady. Above criticality power rises. Control rods absorb neutrons and allow operators to return the reactor to criticality. Delayed neutrons make changes in power slow enough to regulate in normal operation. The heat is carried off by a coolant to raise steam. Thick shielding is needed, and cooling must continue after shutdown. Fermi's first pile used about 350 tonnes of graphite, 37 tonnes of uranium oxide and 6 of uranium metal.
- Pitfalls:
  - Impure graphite: traces of boron stop the reaction (a wrong measurement turned the German project away from graphite)
  - Natural uranium in ordinary water does not work
  - Thinking a reactor can explode like a bomb; the real dangers are radiation, steam or hydrogen explosions and meltdown from decay heat after shutdown
  - Confusing low power with safe exposure: Chicago Pile-1 lacked biological shielding and its first run was deliberately kept at very low power
  - Pulling out control rods quickly near criticality
- History: africa: c. 1.7–2 billion years ago – natural chain reactions in uranium ore at Oklo, Gabon (discovered 1972); americas: 2 December 1942 – Chicago Pile-1 under Enrico Fermi, first controlled, human-made self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction; 1944 Hanford B Reactor starts up; 1948 Oak Ridge uses reactor heat to light a torch bulb; 1951 EBR-I in Idaho powers four light bulbs with electricity from reactor heat; europe: 1939 – Joliot's group in Paris shows that fission releases surplus neutrons; 1954 Obninsk (USSR) feeds a grid; 1956 Calder Hall (Britain), first industrial-scale station
- Read:
  - Enrico Fermi, Experimental Production of a Divergent Chain Reaction, American Journal of Physics 20 (1952)
  - Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
